Diabetes Prediction with Machine Learning (PIMA Indians Diabetes Dataset)¶

Dataset: 768 women of Pima Indian heritage aged 21+, 8 clinical measurements, binary diabetes outcome.

  • Part A – CRISP-DM: business & data understanding, data preparation (missing values, encoding, scaling, outliers)
  • Part B – Features: feature engineering and feature selection (filter, wrapper, embedded) and their impact
  • Part C – Models: 5 classifiers, a PyTorch feed-forward ANN and 5 BMI regressors (each against a baseline)
  • Part D – Evaluation: metrics, learning curves, bias–variance analysis and discussion

Reusable code: data_pipeline.py (cleaning, features), ann.py (neural network), train.py (experiments). python train.py runs the same steps and saves the results used by the Streamlit app.

Part A: CRISP-DM¶

1. Business Understanding¶

  • Goal: predict whether a patient has diabetes (outcome = 1) from 8 routine measurements, to prioritise patients for a confirmatory test.
  • Secondary goal (regression): predict BMI from the other measurements.
  • Success criteria: ROC-AUC (ranking quality) and recall (a missed diabetic is more costly than a false alarm), always compared with a baseline.
  • Constraints: small dataset (768 rows) from a single population (Pima women aged 21+).

2.5 Correlation¶

In [7]:
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6.5))
sns.heatmap(clean.corr(), annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='RdBu_r', vmin=-1, vmax=1)

  • 768 rows, 8 numeric features, 268 positives (34.9%). The data is imbalanced: predicting "no diabetes" for everyone already gives 65.1% accuracy, so ROC-AUC, recall and F1 matter more.
  • Hidden missing values: insulin is 0 in 48.7% of rows and skin thickness in 29.6%; blood pressure (35), BMI (11) and glucose (5) are smaller.
  • Glucose separates the classes best (correlation 0.50 with outcome; median 140 vs 107 mg/dL), followed by BMI (0.31) and insulin (0.30).
  • Insulin and the diabetes pedigree are right-skewed → log transform in Part B.

  • No duplicates and no invalid rows (negative values, non-integer age/pregnancies, wrong outcome).
  • Impossible zeros are now NaN. They are not filled here: imputation is learned inside the model pipeline from training data only, which avoids data leakage.

3.2 Train/Test Split (80/20, stratified)¶

The test set is used once, at the end. Model choice, tuning and thresholds all use 5-fold cross-validation on the training set.

  • 65 outlier values in the training set, mostly diabetes pedigree (19), insulin (17) and blood pressure (13).
  • They are kept: values such as insulin 846 µU/mL or pedigree 2.4 are rare but medically possible, and deleting them would remove real (often high-risk) patients.
  • Their effect is handled instead by median imputation, by testing a RobustScaler (Part B) and by tree models, which are not sensitive to extreme values.

3.4 Preprocessing Pipeline¶

Feature engineering → median imputation + missing-value flags → scaling (numeric) / one-hot encoding (categorical).

  • Missing data: median imputation (robust to the skewed columns) plus missing indicators, because "insulin not measured" can itself carry information.
  • Encoding: the binned features (age band, BMI class) are one-hot encoded.
  • Normalization: StandardScaler for distance/gradient-based models (logistic regression, SVM, ANN); tree models skip scaling.
  • Everything is inside a scikit-learn Pipeline, so in every CV fold the medians and scaling are learned from the training fold only.

  • All three methods keep glucose, and the engineered glucose_x_bmi is the top feature for mutual information (0.161), LASSO (largest coefficient, 0.93) and random-forest importance (0.26).
  • Filter (mutual information) ranks each feature alone; wrapper (RFE) removes the weakest logistic-regression coefficient step by step; embedded (LASSO, L1) sets weak coefficients to exactly 0 and keeps only 7 inputs.
  • The methods disagree on correlated features (e.g. bmi vs bmi_class, age vs age_band), because once one of a pair is kept the other adds little.

6. Impact of Preprocessing, Engineering and Selection¶

One step is added at a time; each row is 5-fold CV repeated 3 times (15 scores) on the training set.

1. Raw data (zeros kept) 0.8299 0.8271 0.0401 0.0421
2. Zeros -> missing + median imputation 0.8399 0.8299 0.0256 0.0370
3. + Standard scaling 0.8337 0.8297 0.0355 0.0374
3b. + Robust scaling (alternative) 0.8405 0.8301 0.0256 0.0370
4. + Feature engineering 0.8442 0.8361 0.0406 0.0358

5. + RFE (wrapper) 0.8443 0.8329 0.0417 0.0398 
Selection method used in Part C: Mutual information (filter)
  • Treating zeros as missing is the most useful cleaning step for logistic regression: 0.830 → 0.840 ROC-AUC, and the spread across folds drops (std 0.040 → 0.026).
  • Scaling does not raise ROC-AUC here (0.834 standard, 0.841 robust), but it is still needed for SVM/ANN and it makes regularisation fair across features. Random forest is unchanged (≈0.830): trees do not need scaling.
  • Feature engineering helps both models: logistic 0.840 → 0.844, random forest 0.830 → 0.836.
  • Selection: mutual information gives the best logistic score (0.849) with 10 of 23 inputs; RFE matches the no-selection score (0.844) and LASSO is slightly lower (0.841). Mutual information is therefore offered as an option to every model in Part C.
  • All gains are small compared with the fold-to-fold std (≈0.03–0.04): on 614 rows preprocessing mostly makes the models more stable, not dramatically better.

Part C: Model Development¶

7. Classification Models¶

Each model is tuned with GridSearchCV (5-fold stratified CV, ROC-AUC). Feature selection is a tuned option (select): the CV decides if it helps.

In [15]:
specs = exp.classifier_specs(exp.SELECTORS[selector])
classifiers, best_params = exp.tune(specs, train[FEATURES], train[TARGET], exp.CV, 'roc_auc')
best_params
Out[15]:
model best_params grid_size
0 Baseline (prior) {} 1
1 Logistic Regression {"C": 0.1, "select": "passthrough"} 8
2 Decision Tree {"max_depth": 5, "min_samples_leaf": 20, "sele... 30
3 Random Forest {"max_depth": 4, "max_features": "sqrt", "min_... 32
4 Gradient Boosting {"learning_rate": 0.03, "max_depth": 2, "n_est... 16
5 SVM (RBF) {"C": 1, "gamma": 0.01, "select": "passthrough"} 12
6 ANN (PyTorch) {"hidden": [32, 16], "weight_decay": 0.0001, "... 8
  • Logistic regression prefers strong regularisation (C = 0.1); the decision tree is limited to depth 5 with ≥20 samples per leaf, and the random forest to depth 4: on small data the CV prefers simpler models.
  • Only gradient boosting keeps the mutual-information filter; for the other models all 23 inputs score better.

8. Neural Network (PyTorch)¶

Feed-forward network: inputs → Dense(32, ReLU) → Dropout(0.2) → Dense(16, ReLU) → Dropout(0.2) → 1 output (sigmoid). Adam optimizer, binary cross-entropy loss, mini-batches of 32, weight decay, early stopping on a 20% validation slice (patience 25).

In [16]:

history.plot(x='epoch', y=['train_accuracy', 'validation_accuracy'], ax=axes[1], title='Accuracy')
for ax in axes:

Best epoch: 19 of 44 run
  • The validation loss is lowest at epoch 19 (0.396) and then starts to rise while the training loss keeps falling: the network begins to overfit, so early stopping restores the epoch-19 weights.
  • Validation accuracy reaches about 82–83%. The (32, 16) network with small weight decay was chosen by CV over the larger (64, 32) one.

9. Regression Models: Predicting BMI¶

BMI is the target, so BMI and the BMI-based features are not inputs; rows without a BMI value are dropped.

Part D: Performance Measurement and Bias–Variance¶

10. Classification Performance¶

  • CV: 5-fold × 3 repeats on the training set → used to pick the best model.
  • Threshold: chosen to maximise F1 on out-of-fold predictions (default 0.5 misses too many diabetics).
  • Test: 154 unseen patients, evaluated once; 95% bootstrap interval for test ROC-AUC.
In [18]:

test_pred = predictions[predictions.split == 'test']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(17, 8))
for ax, name in zip(axes.ravel(), classifiers):
    p = test_pred[test_pred.model == name]

                           display_labels=['No diabetes', 'Diabetes']).plot(cmap='Blues', ax=ax, colorbar=False)

ax = axes.ravel()[-1]

    p = test_pred[test_pred.model == name]
    RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(p.actual, p.probability, name=name, ax=ax, color=MODEL_COLORS[name])
ax.set_title('ROC curves (test)')
ax.legend(fontsize=7)

plt.show()
  • SVM (RBF) has the best CV ROC-AUC (0.847), but logistic regression (0.846) and the ANN (0.843) are statistically the same: the differences are far smaller than the CV std (≈0.03–0.04).
  • On the test set the three are also close: logistic 0.835, ANN 0.828, SVM 0.827 ROC-AUC. All clearly beat the baseline (0.500).
  • With the tuned threshold (0.37), the SVM finds 78% of diabetics (recall) with 76.6% accuracy and F1 0.70; at the default 0.5 the accuracy is 72.1% but more diabetics are missed.
  • The ANN has the highest recall (0.85) at its threshold, at the cost of more false alarms. The decision tree is the weakest real model (test ROC-AUC 0.787).

12.3 Learning Curves¶

In [23]:
curves = exp.learning_curves(classifiers, train, ['Logistic Regression', 'Decision Tree', 'Random Forest', 'ANN (PyTorch)'])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(18, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, c) in zip(axes, curves.groupby('model', sort=False)):
    ax.plot(c.n_train, c.train_roc_auc, 'o-', label='train')
    ax.plot(c.n_train, c.cv_roc_auc, 'o-', label='cross-validation')
    ax.fill_between(c.n_train, c.cv_roc_auc - c.cv_std, c.cv_roc_auc + c.cv_std, alpha=0.2)
    ax.set(title=name, xlabel='training rows', ylim=(0.65, 1.0))
axes[0].set_ylabel('ROC-AUC')
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
  • Decision-tree depth shows the trade-off clearly: depth 1 underfits (CV 0.705, high bias), CV peaks at depth 3 (0.793), and at depth 12 the tree memorises the training set (train 1.000, CV 0.652, high variance).
  • Decision tree (gap 0.09) and random forest (train 0.918 vs CV 0.839, gap 0.08) overfit most → high variance; averaging many trees still keeps the forest's CV score good.
  • Logistic regression, SVM and ANN have small gaps (≈0.02–0.03) → low variance. Their remaining error is mostly bias / noise in the data: their train score is only ≈0.87.
  • Learning curves: for logistic regression and the ANN the CV score still rises from 0.81–0.82 (98 rows) to 0.85 (491 rows), so more data would still help a little; the curves are close together, so more model complexity would not.

13. Which Inputs Drive the Best Model? (permutation importance, test set)¶

In [24]:
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
imp = permutation_importance(classifiers[winner], test[FEATURES], test[TARGET], scoring='roc_auc',
                             n_repeats=30, random_state=dp.SEED)
importance = pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=FEATURES).sort_values()
importance.plot.barh(xerr=imp.importances_std[np.argsort(imp.importances_mean)], figsize=(7, 4),
                     color=SERIES[0], title=f'{winner}: drop in ROC-AUC when a feature is shuffled')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
  • Glucose dominates: shuffling it lowers test ROC-AUC by 0.128. BMI (0.034), age (0.021) and pregnancies (0.014) follow.
  • Skin thickness and insulin add almost nothing once glucose and BMI are known, which matches the selection results in Part B.

14. Synthesis and Discussion¶

How did preprocessing and feature selection affect generalization? Treating impossible zeros as missing (with median imputation and missing flags) was the most valuable step: logistic-regression CV ROC-AUC rose from 0.830 to 0.840 and its fold-to-fold std dropped from 0.040 to 0.026. Feature engineering (log transforms, the glucose × BMI interaction, age and BMI bins) added a further gain for both logistic regression (0.844) and random forest (0.836), and glucose_x_bmi became the top-ranked feature for mutual information, LASSO and random-forest importance. Mutual-information selection gave the best logistic score (0.849) with 10 of 23 inputs. All gains are smaller than the CV std, so on this dataset preprocessing mainly made the models more stable and simpler, while keeping everything inside a pipeline prevented leakage into the test set.

Which model type performed best and why? The RBF SVM had the highest CV ROC-AUC (0.847) and 0.827 on the test set, but logistic regression (CV 0.846, test 0.835) and the ANN (CV 0.843, test 0.828) are equally good within the uncertainty (test 95% CI ≈ 0.75–0.89). For a small, tabular, mostly numeric dataset a smooth decision boundary is enough, so complex models give no extra benefit. Logistic regression is the most practical choice for healthcare: equally accurate, transparent coefficients and the smallest overfitting. For BMI regression, the linear models (Lasso RMSE 5.37, R² 0.43) beat the tree models.

How did dataset size, feature quality and data type influence overfitting? With only 614 training rows, flexible models overfit: a deep tree reaches train ROC-AUC 1.000 but CV 0.652, and even the tuned tree and forest keep train–CV gaps of 0.08–0.09. Feature quality is limited: insulin is missing for 49% of patients and skin thickness for 30%, so these features add noise rather than signal. Because all inputs are numeric and continuous, regularised linear models and small networks fit well, while trees need depth limits (depth 3–5) to generalize. Learning curves show CV scores still rising slowly with more data.

What recommendations would you make for real-world healthcare analytics? (1) Collect more and more diverse data (men, other ethnic groups, other hospitals) and validate externally before use. (2) Prefer interpretable, well-calibrated models and choose the decision threshold with clinicians based on the cost of missed cases, as done here with the F1 threshold (recall 0.78). (3) Record measurements properly instead of storing missing values as 0. (4) Use the model as decision support with clinician review, and monitor its performance and fairness after deployment.

15. Conclusion¶

The complete CRISP-DM pipeline was implemented on the PIMA dataset: cleaning of hidden missing values, outlier analysis, four feature-engineering techniques, three feature-selection methods, five tuned classifiers, a PyTorch ANN and five BMI regressors, evaluated with cross-validation, a held-out test set and bias–variance diagnostics. The trained pipelines are deployed in a Streamlit dashboard (CRISP-DM deployment phase). The best classifiers reach a test ROC-AUC of about 0.83 and, with the tuned threshold, detect about 78% of diabetic patients.
